questions.question: You refactored code between the model and the tools. Why is a live eval a poor way to check nothing changed?
options: Model replies vary run to run, so small behaviour changes hide in noise, and it costs money and time per commit
questions.explanation: Hold the model's side fixed with replay to test your own code's behaviour.

questions.question: What does strict replay check that lenient replay doesn't?
options: That every request sent to the model is identical to the recorded one
questions.explanation: Adding one word to the system prompt was caught at model call 1.

questions.question: During replay, the new code calls issue_refund with an amount that wasn't recorded. What happens?
options: The replay returns 'no recorded result' and the real tool never runs
The replay picks the closest recorded call
questions.explanation: That's both the safety property and the detection signal.

questions.question: Lenient replay of the prompt edit reported 'same' on all tasks. What does that prove?
options: Only that your code behaves the same given the old replies; how the model reacts to the new prompt needs a live eval
questions.explanation: Replay can't show model behaviour changes, because the model's replies are fixed.

questions.question: A-1001 diverged because 79.0 became 79. What should you take from that?
options: Replay keys must normalise exactly as strictly as your tools do; decide whether int vs float matters to the real API
questions.explanation: Too strict a key creates false alarms; too loose a key misses real bugs like 25.5 → 26.

questions.question: A behaviour change is intentional (new refund policy). What do you do with the cassettes?
options: Re-record them with the new version, review the trajectory diff, and commit the new cassettes
questions.explanation: Cassettes encode expected behaviour; when expectations change, refresh them deliberately.
